item.title: Bangladesh hasn't given its students a bargain worth working hard for. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Some years ago, I travelled to Barishal for teaching purposes. That afternoon, a boy in my class mentioned, almost casually, that he had cycled three hours from a remote corner of the district to attend.
Three hours one way, and three hours back that evening, and again the next day. He was not complaining. He simply wanted to learn, and this was the price, so he paid it.
He is not an exception. Multiply him by millions, and you have the students of Bangladesh, fighters in villages and towns across the country.
Thousands of miles away, here in Melbourne, I wake up and see the midnight bulletins from home. This year's Higher Secondary Certificate exams began on July 2, with nearly 1.3 million candidates sitting them, and within two weeks the country was gripped by a fresh wave of Gen Z protests over how those exams were being run.
Torrential rain flooded parts of Chittagong and waterlogged Dhaka, and the Education Ministry pressed on regardless in several districts. Then an audio clip of the education minister went viral, in which he was heard comparing anxious students to "farm chickens" who catch a fever if they get a little wet.
My first instinct, I admit, was the older-generation reflex: Why does every difficulty become a movement? But a deeper thought settled in and would not leave.
Here is what I see from my window in a city that sits near the top of every global liveability ranking. Bangladeshi students, numbering in their thousands, cycling through winter rains at single digit Celsius, delivering meals at midnight, packing shelves before the early morning lectures begin.
Seventy-hour weeks are the norm, and the pay is often not even enough for locals to consider.
Their friends are in Dhaka, a city near the bottom of that same liveability list. They are living at home, eating their mothers' cooking, and they are on the streets, shouting, hopeless.
The same generation, often the same schools, the same para. One half is content grinding through hardship in a foreign winter; the other half cannot bear an exam hall in their own country.
If the problem were laziness, both halves would be lazy. They are not. The problem is something else.
The boy delivering food in Melbourne believes in a simple bargain: If I work, it counts. Hours convert into rent paid, a degree earned, a future that follows knowable rules.
Hardship you choose, in service of a goal you can see, is bearable. It can even feel like dignity.
Humans tolerate enormous suffering they choose, and almost none that is forced on them, with disrespect poured on top.
The student in Dhaka has no such bargain. He has grown up watching question papers leak, syllabuses change like the weather, and merit lost to connections. This year, students demanded not just the minister's resignation but correction of errors, along with fresh exams for those who could not reach flooded centres.
When the exam itself cannot be trusted, it stops being a test and becomes a lottery run by people who hold you in contempt.
Protesting a rigged lottery is not a weakness. It is the only rational move left. The minister eventually apologized in parliament and agreed to arrange retests for affected students, which was itself an admission that the anger had a legitimate core.
My father's generation loves to remind us of its toughness, and fairly so. In his time, they sat two entrance examinations in a single day and walked to the hall barefoot.
Their resilience was real, and today's students should sit with that history honestly. Not every hard question is an injustice; not every discomfort deserves a road blockade. Somewhere in the noise of this movement, that self-reflection must happen too.
But here is what has changed since my father walked barefoot to his exam, and it is not the softness of the young. It is the internet.
His generation endured because they could not see an alternative. This generation scrolls through the alternative every night, watching cousins and classmates abroad work brutal hours and remain hopeful, because effort there buys something. You cannot un-show them that.
This is not the first time such a cycle has occurred. During the mass uprising of 2024, when students attacked the Secretariat building, the government decided to cancel the remainder of the HSC exams altogether, the first time in the nation's history that such an exam was cancelled mid-exam.
While reading the news that day, a title popped into my head: Hajar Bachhor Dhore by Zahir Raihan . For a thousand years, the same water rising, the same voices dismissed, the same loop. A minister mocking a student, a protest, a committee, a compromise, and the loop begins again. We were here in 2024. We will be here next year unless something changes.
That something is a mindset, and it belongs to us, the elders, far more than to the students. The instinct that says we know best, that a student's complaint is an excuse until proven otherwise, that a girl who falls ill in the rain is a farm chicken rather than a child failed by her state.
Every concession the government eventually made, the re-sits, the corrected marks, the suspended paper-setters, quietly admitted the students were right. Offered a week earlier, with respect instead of ridicule, there might have been no movement at all.
Bangladeshi students will work. Melbourne's winter streets prove it every night; the boy from Barishal on his bicycle proved it years ago.
What they will not do, anymore, is work hard for a country that treats their effort as worthless and their voice as noise.
Tahsin Anjum is a PhD Researcher, Swinburne University of Technology, Australia.

item.title: AI will not empty our factories. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh's ready made garment sector employs close to four million people and earns over 80% of the country's export revenue. For four decades, it has been the country's single biggest source of formal work outside the farm. That fact has held so steady for so long that we treat it as permanent. It is not.
The Centre for Policy Dialogue warned this month that up to 1.22 million RMG jobs could disappear by 2041 as automation spreads through the sector , with as much as 60% of current female employment at risk of being wiped out entirely.
The same report found something quieter and more worrying underneath that number. Manufacturing employment across the country has stayed frozen at 8.1 million workers even as production has climbed year after year. The factories are producing more. They are simply not hiring more people to do it.
This is not a distant scenario. Nearly 1.3 million jobs faced cuts throughout Bangladesh in 2024. 90% of that loss fell straight on women , according to official labour data cited in a recent industry report. The report's central complaint was not that automation is happening. It was that no policy exists to manage what happens to the people it displaces.
We are not the only country facing this. Vietnam's textile and garment workers face an even sharper automation risk, with the ILO estimating 86% of jobs in the sector at high risk from robotics and machine driven production .
Vietnam pays its garment workers roughly $300 a month against Bangladesh's $95, so it has less room to compete on labour cost and more reason to compete on output per worker.
Factories there report that automation now lets one worker produce four to five times what they produced before , and the country is pouring money into training programs so its workforce can run and maintain that equipment rather than be replaced by it.
That is the difference between agility and drift. Vietnam is not avoiding automation. It is choosing where automation goes and making sure its own people are the ones operating it.
Bangladesh has largely let automation arrive on its own terms, factory by factory, with no national plan attached to it.
There is genuine opportunity sitting inside this technology if we can capitalize upon it early. A study on AI adoption in Bangladesh's RMG sector has come to a noteworthy finding that real gains are available through better defect detection, demand forecasting, and production planning, the kind of AI applications that raise a factory's output without necessarily cutting its headcount.
The Daily Star has reported that AI powered systems in Bangladeshi factories are already predicting equipment failures before they cause costly downtime and catching stitching flaws faster than a human inspector could. Used this way, AI does not remove the worker from the equation. It removes the waste sitting around her.
But the same study found something that should worry us. Researchers identified a chronic gap between what factories are adopting and what regulation, training systems, and worker protections have prepared for.
There is no clear framework for accountability when an algorithm makes a production decision that costs someone their shift. There is no established path for a machine operator to become a machine technician. The technology is arriving at pace but we are not running them through a strategically agile phase.
Here, strategic agility should mean factories adopting AI for quality control and planning while simultaneously funding the retraining of the workers whose old tasks disappear.
It means vocational training centres building curricula around machine operation and AI assisted production today, not after the job losses have already happened.
It means BGMEA, the labour ministry, and training institutions sitting at the same table before the layoffs, not after them, so that a woman doing manual quality checks this year is doing machine assisted quality control next year instead of leaving the workforce altogether.
None of this is unfamiliar territory for Bangladesh. Our history tells us that we know how to move when the underlying economics forces our hand. AI is forcing our hand right now. The choice now is whether we plan for the workers standing next to it, or wait until the next report tells us how many of them are gone.
Nafis Ehsas Chowdhury works at M M Ispahani Limited.

item.title: Allow prices to do their work. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We may not like how prices work. We may greatly prefer that the outcome was something different. But it is true that prices work.
This is the point that is at the heart of free market economics. Let us have the prices -- the things that work -- and thus the economy that works.
The parts we do not like about the results, we can clean up if that's what we want to do.
For example, the free market might lead to some people having more money than others. Well, OK. Maybe we're OK with that, maybe we're not.
If we're not, we can tax the richer people and give the money to the poorer. Not that I would recommend that but it is, obviously, possible.
But this is something done after the free markets and prices have been allowed to work. This is, largely enough, how that social democracy of the Nordic countries works.
They are more free market, even more capitalist, than most of Europe and even the US. But then they have higher taxes and more redistribution.
As I say, that's not what I would do, the redistribution, but it does work. You have rich places still getting richer under such a system. Because the market is allowed to work first, to create the wealth that can then be redistributed.
As opposed to a system where the bureaucracy decides that prices cannot be allowed to work, and therefore the economy doesn't create the wealth that can then be collected.
This is the starting point for talking about the gas shortage in Bangladesh. As this newspaper reports , there is an energy crisis in industry. The energy deficit is becoming a macroeconomic problem . Factories have to close simply because there is not the natural gas to keep them running.
As is so often true, the problem now is that we were not doing things the right way in the past. This does not help us a great deal right now, but it does inform what we should be doing now in order to have fewer problems in the future.
We should allow energy prices to be free market. As I said back in March this year in fact. I agree, this does not help us very much right now. But getting the right underlying policies now means fewer of those problems in the future.
So, what this means is no allocation of energy by the government. No pricing of energy by the government. And the true meaning of “free market” is that it is free of bureaucracy, of permissions, to enter the market.
So, if someone wants to drill for gas in the Bay of Bengal, they can. Or on land. Or build another, or more, LNG terminals. Or, of course, build out solar panels, or windmills, or any other energy provision service they desire to throw their money at.
Leave the market be that is. Allow prices to do their work.
The argument against this is that at times, poor people -- or some factories -- will not be able to afford the energy. Yet, for poor people the solution is simple -- give poor people some more money so as to be able to afford the energy.
For factories that have to close, what's different from what is happening now? Factories are closing because there is no energy, not just because energy is expensive.
The very beating heart of this argument is that markets -- and the freer the better -- work very well. Except for that one little thing, sometimes we do not like the results of reality working as it does through markets.
The correct solution to this is to still use the markets but then adjust the results. Instead of what happens all-too-often, which is to insist that as markets produce undesirable outcomes, therefore we must use planning and bureaucracy instead.
Which is what leads to what we have now -- bad results but no way of solving them. For we do still have factories closing because there is no energy to run them.
It is entirely true that markets are not perfect and that we'd sometimes like the results to be different. That's fine, as long as we run with this rule -- markets first, adjust the result later.
Tim Worstall is a senior fellow at the Adam Smith Institute in London.
